opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there's a tendency to think of robotics as kind of an application area: you build these really powerful AI systems, language models and so on, and then at the end you bolt them onto a robot and get it to do useful stuff. But I actually think it's the other way around in some important sense. The physical world is where intelligence came from in the first place. Humans, animals, we all developed our cognitive abilities because we had to deal with a messy, unstructured physical environment, and that's what grounds a lot of our understanding of the world.

The other piece is that, from a pure machine learning perspective, the thing that made language models work so well is generality. You train one model on an enormous breadth of data and it picks up all sorts of things that a narrow model never would. Robotics historically has been the opposite of that. Every lab builds a system for one robot, one task, one environment, and it doesn't transfer. So the question for us is: can you get the same kind of effect where you train one model across many robots and many tasks, and it becomes better at each individual thing because it's seen all the others? What we've seen so far suggests that yes, it really does work that way. Cross-embodiment data helps, and the model starts to show some of the same emergent generalization we see in language.

And then if you can get that working, it's not just about robots folding laundry, although that's great too. It's about having AI systems that actually understand cause and effect in the physical world, that can learn from their own experience and interaction rather than just from passively scraped text. I think that kind of embodied learning loop is going to be pretty essential for getting to really capable AI, so that's why I see it as central rather than peripheral.

r001.rationale: The response argues robotics is central to capable AI and discusses generalizing across robots and tasks, but does not say general-purpose robotics encompasses essentially all AI technology.

r002.rationale: It mentions robots folding laundry and physical-world learning, but does not suggest a truly general robot could do a large portion of what people can do.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I see it is that if you want to understand intelligence, and if you want to build systems that are truly intelligent in the way that humans and animals are intelligent, you have to grapple with the fact that intelligence evolved to control bodies in the physical world. Everything else that we think of as the hallmarks of intelligence, language, abstract reasoning, planning, all of that came later, and it came on top of a system whose original job was to figure out where to put your hands and your feet so that you don't fall over and you can get food.

So when we talk about AI as a general problem, I think it's actually a little strange that for the past several years the most capable systems we've built are ones that live entirely in a world of text. They're incredibly impressive, but they've basically learned about the world secondhand, through what humans have written about it. And there's a lot that's just not written down. Nobody writes down how much force to use when you pick up a paper cup versus a glass, or how a shirt deforms when you grab it by the collar. That's the stuff you learn by actually interacting with the world, and that's the stuff that robots have to learn.

The reason I frame it as foundation models specifically, rather than just robotics, is that I think the lesson from language and vision has been pretty clear: the thing that works is to train large models on broad, diverse data, and then let those models generalize and be adapted to lots of downstream tasks. For a long time, robotics didn't do that. Every lab had its own robot, its own task, its own small dataset, and you'd train a policy that worked in one room on one object and then it would fall apart if you moved the table six inches. That's not a path to general intelligence. The bet with robotic foundation models is that if you pool together experience across many robots, many tasks, many environments, and you combine that with the knowledge that's already in vision-language models, you start to get something that has the same kind of flexibility we see in other domains.

And I'd actually go a step further. I think the physical world is in some sense the ultimate test of whether a model's understanding is real. In text, you can get a long way with plausibility, with producing something that sounds right. In the physical world, the cup either gets picked up or it doesn't. The laundry either gets folded or it ends up on the floor. There's a kind of grounding there that I think is essential, not just for robots to be useful, but for AI systems in general to actually have a correct model of how the world works. So I don't see robotics as an application of AI that we get to once the hard problems are solved. I think it is one of the hard problems, and maybe the one that forces us to confront what we actually mean by general intelligence.

r001.rationale: The response calls robotics a fundamental part of AI and a hard problem, but does not state that general-purpose robotics encompasses essentially all AI technology.

r002.rationale: It discusses robots learning physical tasks such as picking up cups and folding laundry, but does not suggest a truly general robot could perform a large portion of what people can do.

astra-6.text:
I think the central question is whether we want AI systems that can actually interact with the world, or systems that can answer questions about it. Those are closely related capabilities, but they’re not quite the same thing.

When you interact with the world, you have to reason about how your actions will change it. You have to deal with uncertainty, gather information, and recover when something doesn’t go the way you expected. Robotics gives us a very concrete setting in which to study those problems. You can describe how to pick up a glass perfectly well, but if you actually try to do it, you have to contend with where the glass is, how slippery it is, whether it’s full. Your understanding has to support action.

The reason the general-purpose part matters is that we don’t want to engineer a separate solution for every object and every task. We want a system that can draw on experience across many different situations and use that experience to do something new. That’s very much the same ambition that motivates foundation models in language.

And I don’t think this necessarily means that every intelligent system needs a robot body. But learning how to act, how to discover the consequences of your actions, and how to improve through experience seems like a fundamental part of the AI problem. Physical robots are one particularly demanding—and useful—way to confront that.

r001.rationale: The response calls robotics a useful setting for studying action and learning, but does not say it encompasses essentially all AI technology.

r002.rationale: It describes using experience to handle new situations, but does not claim a truly general robot could perform a large portion of what people can do.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is whether intelligence is something that we build to answer questions, or something that allows an agent to interact with the world and accomplish goals. Robotics forces us to confront that second version of the problem. You have to perceive what’s going on, decide what to do, take an action, and then deal with the consequences of that action.

What makes a general-purpose model interesting is that these capabilities shouldn’t have to be rebuilt for every task. A robot that has learned to clean up a kitchen should bring something useful to learning how to organize a workshop. It needs some understanding of objects, of physical interactions, and of how its actions change the world. The question is how to acquire that understanding in a way that transfers.

And there’s a connection here to learning itself. Humans don’t learn everything from descriptions of what other people have done. We try things. We discover that our expectations were wrong, and we adjust. A robotic system gives us a very concrete setting in which to study that process: how an intelligent system can acquire knowledge through its own experience, rather than only absorb knowledge that’s already been written down.

r001.rationale: The response presents robotics as a setting for studying intelligence and learning, but does not say general-purpose robotics encompasses essentially all AI technology.

r002.rationale: It gives examples of transferring skills between robot tasks, but does not claim a general robot could perform a large portion of what people can do.
